topicName: JVM Heap, Garbage Collection, and OS Settings
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"JVM Heap, Garbage Collection, and OS Settings in Elasticsearch"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Properly tuning the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and operating system settings is critical for running a stable and high-performance Elasticsearch cluster. Incorrect configurations can lead to OutOfMemory (OOM) errors, excessive garbage collection pauses, and degraded node performance."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Elasticsearch JVM Heap Sizing"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Elasticsearch runs on the JVM and relies heavily on heap memory for caching, query execution, and indexing operations. However, sizing the heap correctly requires balancing application needs with the underlying host memory."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Rule of Thumb: Never allocate more than 50% of the available system RAM to the Elasticsearch JVM heap, ensuring the other half remains free for the operating system page cache."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The 32GB Ceiling: Keep the JVM heap below 32GB if possible. Compressed ordinary object pointers (Compressed Oops) allow the JVM to use 32-bit references on 64-bit platforms, saving significant memory. Exceeding 32GB disables this feature and increases memory overhead."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"-Xms31g\n-Xmx31g"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Garbage Collection (GC) Configuration"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern versions of Elasticsearch ship with the Java 11 or Java 17 runtime bundled, utilizing the Garbage-First (G1GC) garbage collector by default. G1GC is designed to meet soft real-time garbage collection goals with high probability while maintaining high throughput."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Initiating GC Threshold: G1GC initiates mixed garbage collection cycles when the heap reaches a certain occupancy threshold, controlled via settings such as initiatingHeapOccupancyPercent."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitoring: Regularly monitor GC logs to detect 'Stop-The-World' pauses that can cause nodes to drop out of the Elasticsearch cluster due to missed heartbeat responses (zen discovery timeout)."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Critical Operating System Settings"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"The operating system plays a vital role in keeping Elasticsearch stable. Failing to configure OS parameters can result in unstable nodes, swapping, and low file descriptor limits."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Disable Swapping: Swapping JVM heap to disk severely degrades performance and causes node instability. You must disable swap entirely or set vm.swappiness to 1."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"sudo swapoff -a"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Memory Locking: Use bootstrap.memory_lock: true in elasticsearch.yml combined with disabling swap to ensure the JVM heap never gets swapped out to disk."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"File Descriptors: Elasticsearch opens many files and indices simultaneously. Increase the maximum number of open file descriptors for the elasticsearch user, typically to at least 65535."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"elasticsearch soft nofile 65535\nelasticsearch hard nofile 65535"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Virtual Memory: Elasticsearch uses a hybrid of mmapfs directories to store its indices. Ensure the operating system allows enough virtual memory maps for these files."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144"}]
